name: Assets-to-market (top 10 by total assets / market cap, monthly)
thesis: Firms with high total assets relative to market value earn higher subsequent returns (Fama & French 1992, Journal of Finance), a value measure that uses the whole balance sheet rather than book equity. Chen & Zimmermann's Open Source Asset Pricing catalogue (signal AM) replicates it with t = 5.69. Total assets is the latest instant filed with the SEC; market cap is close x filed shares, both point in time.
kill_criteria: it selects the same names as book-to-market (batch 2) and is that strategy again with leverage added, so the two results are one draw, not two
the top ten by assets-to-market are the most levered balance sheets in the universe, and the result is a leverage bet that tracks credit conditions rather than value

name: Low book leverage (bottom 10 by total assets / book equity, monthly)
thesis: Firms with lower book leverage, total assets over book equity, earn higher subsequent returns once market leverage is held apart (Fama & French 1992, Journal of Finance; catalogue signal BookLeverage, sign negative, t = 5.34). The published equity adds deferred taxes and preferred stock to shareholder equity; here it is filed stockholders' equity alone, which is the catalogue's first-choice definition.
kill_criteria: negative book equity makes the ratio negative and sorts a distressed firm as the least levered, so any name the book holds with negative equity invalidates the result
the effect is the mirror of the assets-to-market spec and moves with it, making the pair one hypothesis measured twice

name: Market leverage (top 10 by total liabilities / market cap, monthly)
thesis: Firms with high total liabilities relative to market equity earn higher subsequent returns beyond what beta explains (Bhandari 1988, Journal of Finance; catalogue signal Leverage, t = 3.93). The firm does not store total liabilities, so it is taken as total assets minus stockholders' equity, the balance-sheet identity; this counts minority interest as a liability, which is the one deviation.
kill_criteria: the most levered names are banks-adjacent and utilities, so the result is a rate-sensitivity bet that turns with the yield curve rather than a leverage premium
it holds nearly the same names as assets-to-market, since both divide a balance-sheet total by market cap

name: Cash flow to price (top 10 by operating cash flow / market cap, monthly)
thesis: Firms with high operating cash flow relative to market value outperform, and cash flow is a cleaner value signal than earnings because accruals do not inflate it (Desai, Rajgopal & Venkatachalam 2004, The Accounting Review; catalogue signal cfp, t = 2.77). Operating cash flow is the latest annual figure filed with the SEC.
kill_criteria: it selects the same names as earnings yield (batch 2), which failed with IR -0.57, and fails with it for the same reason
the cash-rich top ten are mature mega-caps whose run is the index's run, so the active return is near zero across folds

name: Book equity growth (bottom 10 by year-on-year growth, monthly)
thesis: Firms whose book equity grows slowest subsequently outperform those whose equity grows fastest, the equity-side counterpart of the asset-growth effect (Lockwood & Prombutr 2010, Journal of Financial Research; catalogue signal ChEQ, sign negative, t = 5.38). The paper includes a firm only when book equity is positive in both years; the growth feature drops a non-positive prior year, but a firm whose equity turned negative this year is still ranked, which is the deviation.
kill_criteria: it holds the same names as asset growth (batch 2) because equity and assets grow together, so the two are one investment-factor draw
the slowest equity growers are firms buying back stock heavily, and the result is a buyback effect rather than an investment one

name: Operating leverage (top 10 by operating costs / total assets, monthly)
thesis: Firms with high operating costs relative to assets carry more operating leverage and earn higher returns as compensation for that risk (Novy-Marx 2011, Review of Finance; catalogue signal OPLeverage, t = 3.38). The paper uses cost of goods sold plus SG&A. The firm stores neither, so costs are taken as revenue minus operating income, which also counts depreciation and R&D; that is the deviation, and it tilts the score toward R&D-heavy firms.
kill_criteria: the substitute cost measure makes this an R&D-intensity bet in disguise, and it tracks the R&D spec (batch 2) rather than operating leverage
the high-cost names are low-margin retailers and airlines whose returns follow consumer demand, a cyclical bet with one good fold

name: Change in asset turnover (top 10, monthly)
thesis: An improvement in asset turnover, sales per dollar of assets, predicts higher subsequent returns because the market underreacts to changes in operating efficiency (Soliman 2008, The Accounting Review; catalogue signal ChAssetTurnover, t = 5.12). The change is approximated as revenue growth minus asset growth, which equals the proportional change in turnover to first order; the paper uses the level difference, which is the deviation.
kill_criteria: revenue growth dominates the difference and the book is a sales-growth bet, which the literature finds overpriced rather than underpriced
a single acquisition moves both revenue and assets in one year and puts the acquirer at the top for reasons unrelated to efficiency

name: Percent accruals (bottom 10 by (net income - operating cash flow) / |net income|, monthly)
thesis: Scaling accruals by the size of earnings rather than by assets identifies the firms whose profits are mostly accounting, and low percent-accrual firms outperform high ones (Hafzalla, Lundholm & Van Winkle 2011, The Accounting Review; catalogue signal PctAcc, sign negative, t = 3.29). Unlike the assets-scaled accrual spec (batch 2), this ranks on how much of each firm's own earnings is accrual.
kill_criteria: near-zero net income makes the ratio explode, so one firm with tiny earnings dominates each rebalance and the result is that name's return
it selects the same names as the assets-scaled accrual spec, which scored IR 0.11, and adds nothing to it

name: Return on assets (top 10 by net income / total assets, monthly)
thesis: More profitable firms, by return on assets, earn higher subsequent returns, and the effect is strongest right after the figure is reported (Balakrishnan, Bartov & Faurel 2010, Journal of Accounting and Economics; catalogue signal roaq, t = 6.45). The paper uses quarterly income over lagged quarterly assets. The firm stores annual figures only, so this is annual net income over current total assets, a slower and staler version of the signal; that is the main deviation.
kill_criteria: the annual figure is up to a year old by the time it ranks, and the published effect is concentrated in the weeks after a quarterly report, so the edge is gone in the annual version
it selects the same profitable mega-caps as gross profitability (batch 2) and is that strategy with a noisier numerator
